claim: CIRL is expressed in Drosophila larval chordotonal organs (ChOs), mechanosensory structures that respond to gentle touch, sound, and proprioceptive input.
source: CIRL (ADGRL/Latrophilin, Lphn), one of the oldest members of the aGPCR family, is expressed in the neuronal dendrites and cilia of Drosophila larval chordotonal organs (ChOs), mechanosensory structures that respond to gentle touch, sound, and proprioceptive input (Kernan, 2007; Scholz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kernan, 2007; Scholz et al., 2015) that established CIRL expression in ChOs.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of CIRL triggers a conformational change of the protein and activation via its tethered agonist (Stachel).
source: Here, mechanical stimulation of CIRL triggers a conformational change of the protein and activation via its tethered agonist (Stachel) (Liebscher et al., 2014; Stoveken et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Liebscher et al., 2014; Stoveken et al., 2015) that demonstrated the tethered agonist activation mechanism.

claim: Signalling by activated CIRL reduces intracellular cAMP levels in chordotonal organs.
source: Signalling by the activated receptor reduces intracellular cAMP levels, which in turn sensitizes ChO neurons and potentiates the mechanically-evoked receptor potential (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that demonstrated CIRL's effect on cAMP levels in ChO neurons.

claim: CIRL sensitizes ChO neurons and potentiates the mechanically-evoked receptor potential.
source: Signalling by the activated receptor reduces intracellular cAMP levels, which in turn sensitizes ChO neurons and potentiates the mechanically-evoked receptor potential (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that demonstrated CIRL's sensitizing effect on ChO neurons.

claim: Cirl is transcribed in md neurons in addition to ChOs.
source: Previous work demonstrated prominent expression of Cirl in ChOs, where it modulates sensory processing of innocuous mechanical stimuli (Scholz et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2017). In addition, Cirl transcription was also noted in md neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Scholz et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2017) that noted Cirl transcription in md neurons.

claim: C4da neurons are polymodal nociceptors that respond to noxious temperatures, intense light, and harsh mechanical touch.
source: Motivated by this observation, we now turned our attention to C4da neurons: polymodal nociceptors, which respond to noxious temperatures, intense light and, importantly, harsh mechanical touch (Tracey et al., 2003; Xiang et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Kim and Johnson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Tracey et al., 2003; Xiang et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Kim and Johnson, 2014) that characterized C4da neurons as polymodal nociceptors.

claim: Cirl is expressed in both ppk-negative ChOs and ppk-positive C4da neurons.
source: This setting revealed Cirl transcription in both ppk-negative ChOs and ppk-positive C4da neurons (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1, which displays immunohistochemical staining showing Cirl promoter-driven expression in both ChOs and C4da neurons.

claim: Cirl null mutants (dCirlKO) show significantly increased nocifensive behaviour compared to control larvae when stimulated with a 40 mN von Frey filament.
source: Mechanical stimulation with a 40 mN von Frey filament triggered nocifensive behaviour in 53% of control larvae. In contrast, Cirl null mutants (dCirlKO) showed significantly increased nocifensive behaviour and responded in 75% of the trials (Figure 2B; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and Table 1, showing quantified nocifensive responses in control vs. dCirlKO larvae.

claim: Knocking-down Cirl levels specifically in C4da neurons via RNA-interference (ppk-GAL4 >UAS-dCirlRNAi) phenocopies the Cirl null mutant.
source: Knocking-down Cirl levels specifically in C4da neurons via RNA-interference (RNAi; ppk-GAL4 >UAS-dCirlRNAi) delivered a mutant phenocopy and re-expressing Cirl in nociceptors rescued the mutant phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that RNAi knockdown in C4da neurons produces the same phenotype as the null mutant.

claim: Re-expressing Cirl in nociceptors rescues the dCirlKO mutant phenotype.
source: Knocking-down Cirl levels specifically in C4da neurons via RNA-interference (RNAi; ppk-GAL4 >UAS-dCirlRNAi) delivered a mutant phenocopy and re-expressing Cirl in nociceptors rescued the mutant phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing genetic rescue of the mutant phenotype.

claim: Cirl overexpression in C4da neurons results in diminished nocifensive responses.
source: Notably, Cirl overexpression had the opposite effect resulting in diminished nocifensive responses (Figure 2B; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and Table 1, showing reduced nocifensive behavior with Cirl overexpression.

claim: CIRL curtails mechanical nociception by carrying out a cell-autonomous, dose-dependent function in C4da neurons.
source: These results show that CIRL curtails mechanical nociception by carrying out a cell-autonomous, dose-dependent function in C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that Cirl knockdown, knockout, and overexpression in C4da neurons produce dose-dependent effects on nocifensive behavior.

claim: Optogenetic activation of bPAC in C4da neurons (ppk-GAL4 >UAS-bPAC) leads to increased nocifensive behaviour during blue light exposure.
source: Indeed, driving bPAC in C4da neurons (ppk-GAL4 >UAS-bPAC) led to increased nocifensive behaviour during light exposure, whereas control animals showed no light-induced effects (Figure 3B; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and Table 2, showing light-induced nocifensive behavior in bPAC-expressing larvae.

claim: bPAC expression produces some irregular behaviour in the absence of photostimulation ('spontaneous bending'), likely due to the enzyme's residual dark activity.
source: Notably, bPAC expression also produced some irregular behaviour in the absence of photostimulation ('spontaneous bending'; Figure 3B), which is likely a result of the enzyme's residual dark activity (Stierl et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation (Figure 3B) and a citation to prior work (Stierl et al., 2011) characterizing bPAC's dark activity.

claim: Nocifensive responses are further enhanced by bPAC in dCirlKO larvae (dCirlKO ppk-GAL4 >UAS-bPAC), consistent with increased cAMP levels in mutant C4da neurons.
source: Nocifensive responses were further enhanced by bPAC in dCirlKO larvae (dCirlKO ppk-GAL4 >UAS-bPAC), in line with increased cAMP levels in mutant C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing additive effects of bPAC and Cirl mutation, and inferred to be consistent with elevated cAMP in the mutant.

claim: Larvae carrying mutant alleles of the phosphodiesterase dunce show pronounced nocifensive behaviour that accompanies chronically elevated cAMP concentrations.
source: Independent support for this conclusion was received by analysing larvae carrying mutant alleles of the phosphodiesterase (PDE) dunce (Davis and Kiger, 1981). Here, pronounced nocifensive behaviour accompanies chronically elevated cAMP concentrations (Figure 3C; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C and Table 1, and a citation to prior work (Davis and Kiger, 1981) characterizing dunce mutants.

claim: The adenylyl cyclase inhibitors SQ22536 and DDA significantly decrease nocifensive behaviour of Drosophila larvae.
source: Consistent with nociceptor sensitization by cAMP, dietary supplementation with the adenylyl cyclase inhibitors SQ22536 or DDA (2',3'-dideoxyadenosine) significantly decreased nocifensive behaviour of Drosophila larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced nocifensive behavior with adenylyl cyclase inhibitor treatment.

claim: Adenylyl cyclase inhibitor treatment produces the same nocifensive responses in control and dCirlKO animals to von Frey filament stimulation.
source: Importantly, this treatment produced the same responses of control and dCirlKO animals to von Frey filament stimulation (Figure 3D; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D and Table 1, showing that adenylyl cyclase inhibition eliminates the difference between control and mutant.

claim: CIRL acts in the same pathway as cAMP production by the adenylyl cyclase.
source: This result shows that CIRL acts in the same pathway as cAMP production by the adenylyl cyclase and supports the notion that the aGPCR exerts its antinociceptive effect by lowering cAMP levels through Gi/o -mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental result that adenylyl cyclase inhibition eliminates the phenotypic difference between control and dCirlKO animals.

claim: CIRL exerts its antinociceptive effect by lowering cAMP levels through Gi/o-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: This result shows that CIRL acts in the same pathway as cAMP production by the adenylyl cyclase and supports the notion that the aGPCR exerts its antinociceptive effect by lowering cAMP levels through Gi/o -mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that CIRL acts in the cAMP pathway and that elevated cAMP increases nociceptor activity.

claim: dCirlRNAi significantly enhances calcium responses to noxious mechanical stimulation in C4da neurons.
source: Consistent with the behavioural data describing a CIRL-mediated downregulation of nociceptor function, dCirlRNAi significantly enhanced calcium responses to noxious mechanical stimulation (Figure 4A,B; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 4A,B and Table 1, showing increased GCaMP6m signals in dCirlRNAi neurons.

claim: dCirlKO larvae respond more strongly than controls to photostimulation of C4da neurons via ChR2XXM over a range of different blue light intensities.
source: Notably, dCirlKO larvae (dCirlKO ppk-GAL4 >UAS-chop2XXM) responded more strongly than controls (ppk-GAL4 >UAS-chop2XXM) over a range of different blue light intensities (475 nm; Figure 4C; Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in Figure 4C and Table 3, showing dose-dependent photoinduced responses.

claim: CIRL decreases the excitability of mechanical nociceptors.
source: This demonstrates that CIRL decreases the excitability of mechanical nociceptors, contrasting its role in touch-sensitive neurons where the aGPCR specifically enhances mechanotransduction (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the optogenetic experiment showing that CIRL affects responses to direct neuronal activation (bypassing mechanotransduction), and contrasted with prior work (Scholz et al., 2017).

claim: CIRL specifically enhances mechanotransduction in touch-sensitive neurons.
source: This demonstrates that CIRL decreases the excitability of mechanical nociceptors, contrasting its role in touch-sensitive neurons where the aGPCR specifically enhances mechanotransduction (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that demonstrated CIRL's role in mechanotransduction in ChO neurons.

claim: The dCirlT>A allele carries a mutation at the +1 position of the GPS within the Stachel sequence.
source: Whereas the dCirlT>A allele carries a mutation at the +1 position of the GPS within the Stachel sequence, the −2 mutation in the dCirlH>A allele leaves the Stachel intact but reduces protein expression (Figure 4D; Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the mutant alleles and a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that characterized these mutations.

claim: The −2 mutation in the dCirlH>A allele leaves the Stachel intact but reduces protein expression.
source: Whereas the dCirlT>A allele carries a mutation at the +1 position of the GPS within the Stachel sequence, the −2 mutation in the dCirlH>A allele leaves the Stachel intact but reduces protein expression (Figure 4D; Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the mutant alleles and a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that characterized these mutations.

claim: The dCirlT>A allele shows normal nocifensive responses.
source: Our analysis of nocifensive behaviour in these mutants reported normal responses for the T > A allele and a CirlKO phenocopy for the H > A allele (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 4E and Table 1, showing that the T>A mutation does not affect nocifensive behavior.

claim: The dCirlH>A allele phenocopies CirlKO in nocifensive behaviour.
source: Our analysis of nocifensive behaviour in these mutants reported normal responses for the T > A allele and a CirlKO phenocopy for the H > A allele (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 4E and Table 1, showing that the H>A mutation produces the same phenotype as the null mutant.

claim: C4da neurons are sensitive to reduced CIRL expression.
source: Thus, C4da neurons appear to be sensitive to reduced CIRL expression, which is consistent with very low protein levels in wild-type animals (close to the detection threshold; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the H>A mutant phenotype and supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing low CIRL protein levels.

claim: An intact tethered agonist is dispensable for CIRL function in mechanical nociceptors.
source: An intact tethered agonist, in turn, is dispensable for CIRL function in mechanical nociceptors, contrasting the situation in touch-sensitive ChO neurons, where mutating the Stachel sequence disrupts receptor function (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal nocifensive behavior of the dCirlT>A mutant (which disrupts the Stachel) and contrasted with prior work (Scholz et al., 2017).

claim: Mutating the Stachel sequence disrupts CIRL receptor function in touch-sensitive ChO neurons.
source: An intact tethered agonist, in turn, is dispensable for CIRL function in mechanical nociceptors, contrasting the situation in touch-sensitive ChO neurons, where mutating the Stachel sequence disrupts receptor function (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that demonstrated the requirement for an intact Stachel in ChO neurons.

claim: The activation mechanism of CIRL differs for the two mechanosensory submodalities (touch-sensitive neurons vs. nociceptors).
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the activation mechanism of CIRL differs for the two mechanosensory submodalities.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential requirement for the Stachel sequence in ChO neurons vs. C4da neurons.

claim: The chemotherapeutic agent paclitaxel causes dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy in patients.
source: The chemotherapeutic agent paclitaxel, employed to treat solid tumours such as ovarian or breast cancer, causes dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy in patients.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about paclitaxel's side effects.

claim: Feeding Drosophila larvae paclitaxel-supplemented food induces axonal injury and degeneration of C4da neurons.
source: Similarly, feeding Drosophila larvae paclitaxel-supplemented food induces axonal injury and degeneration of C4da neurons (Bhattacharya et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Bhattacharya et al., 2012) that established this Drosophila neuropathy model.

claim: Paclitaxel strongly enhances nocifensive responses of control larvae.
source: Consistent with chemotherapy-induced allodynia in humans, paclitaxel strongly enhanced nocifensive responses of control larvae (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A, showing increased nocifensive behavior after paclitaxel treatment.

claim: Paclitaxel produces a comparable enhancement of nocifensive responses in dCirlKO animals as in controls.
source: We observed a comparable effect in dCirlKO animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing similar paclitaxel-induced increases in nocifensive behavior in both control and dCirlKO larvae.

claim: Overexpressing Cirl reverts the paclitaxel-induced sensitization of C4da neurons.
source: Overexpressing Cirl, in turn, reverted the paclitaxel-induced sensitization of C4da neurons (Figure 5A; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A and Table 1, showing that Cirl overexpression prevents paclitaxel-induced increases in nocifensive behavior.

claim: CIRL tones down nociceptors in both physiological and neuropathic hyperexcitable states.
source: Thus, CIRL tones down nociceptors in both physiological and neuropathic hyperexcitable states.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that CIRL reduces nociceptor activity under both normal conditions and after paclitaxel treatment.

claim: Paclitaxel administration causes dendrite loss in wild-type C4da neurons and in nociceptors overexpressing Cirl.
source: Following paclitaxel treatment (10 µM), we observed dendrite loss in the wild-type background and in nociceptors overexpressing Cirl (Figure 5B,C; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric data presented in Figure 5B,C and Table 1, showing reduced dendritic complexity after paclitaxel treatment.

claim: Elevated Cirl expression itself reduces the dendritic complexity of C4da neurons.
source: In fact, elevated Cirl expression itself reduced the dendritic complexity of C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric data showing that Cirl overexpression alone reduces dendritic complexity.

claim: Increasing CIRL protein copy number counteracts the neuropathic hyperexcitability of mechanical nociceptors independently of neuropathy-associated morphological defects.
source: Thus, increasing CIRL protein copy number counteracts the neuropathic hyperexcitability of mechanical nociceptors independently of neuropathy-associated morphological defects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Cirl overexpression reduces paclitaxel-induced hyperexcitability despite also causing dendritic loss.

claim: Modulation of nociceptor physiology by CIRL is not tightly coupled to morphological changes.
source: Consistent with the interpretation that modulation of nociceptor physiology by CIRL is not tightly coupled to morphological changes, dCirlKO C4da neurons displayed only subtle structural alterations (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dCirlKO neurons show altered physiology but minimal morphological changes, as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Unilateral chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the sciatic nerve in rats develops thermal hypersensitivity and mechanical allodynia.
source: This model resembles paclitaxel-induced neuropathy in the development of thermal hypersensitivity and mechanical allodynia (Sisignano et al., 2016), i.e. a noxious reaction to innocuous stimuli like touch, reaching a maximum after one week (Figure 6A; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sisignano et al., 2016) and experimental data in Figure 6A and Table 1 showing mechanical allodynia after CCI.

claim: Cirl1 and Cirl3 are expressed in mouse DRG nociceptors according to RNA sequencing data.
source: According to RNA sequencing data from mouse DRG neurons, Cirl1 and Cirl3 are expressed in nociceptors (Thakur et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior RNA sequencing work (Thakur et al., 2014) that identified Cirl1 and Cirl3 expression in nociceptors.

claim: Cirl1 mRNA levels are significantly reduced in isolectin-B4 (IB4)-positive, non-peptidergic nociceptors one week after CCI.
source: Interestingly, Cirl1 mRNA probes described significantly reduced transcript levels in isolectin-B4 (IB4)-positive, non-peptidergic nociceptors one week after CCI (Figure 6B,D,E; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6B,D,E and Table 1, showing reduced Cirl1 expression in IB4-positive neurons after CCI.

claim: A similar, though statistically insignificant trend of reduced Cirl1 expression is observed in peptidergic nociceptors identified by CGRP staining after CCI.
source: We observed a similar, though statistically insignificant trend in peptidergic nociceptors identified by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) staining and for Cirl3 probes (Figure 6B-E; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6B-E and Table 1, showing a non-significant trend toward reduced Cirl1 in CGRP-positive neurons.

claim: A similar, though statistically insignificant trend of reduced expression is observed for Cirl3 probes after CCI.
source: We observed a similar, though statistically insignificant trend in peptidergic nociceptors identified by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) staining and for Cirl3 probes (Figure 6B-E; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6B-E and Table 1, showing a non-significant trend toward reduced Cirl3 expression.

claim: CCI does not affect Cirl1 or Cirl3 gene expression in non-nociceptive, large myelinated neurons marked by neurofilament protein NF200.
source: Notably, CCI appeared to neither affect Cirl1 nor Cirl3 gene expression in non-nociceptive, large myelinated neurons marked by neurofilament protein NF200.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing no significant change in Cirl1 or Cirl3 expression in NF200-positive neurons after CCI.

claim: The correlative results from rat DRG are consistent with the Drosophila data linking low Cirl expression levels to nociceptor sensitization.
source: These correlative results are consistent with the Drosophila data linking low Cirl expression levels to nociceptor sensitization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between reduced Cirl1 expression and allodynia in rats, which parallels the Drosophila findings.

claim: Drosophila larvae display a stereotyped nocifensive response to noxious mechanical insult characterized by a 'corkscrew' body roll.
source: Drosophila larvae display a stereotyped response to noxious mechanical insult. Importantly, this innate nocifensive behaviour, characterized by a 'corkscrew' body roll, can be quantified and is distinct from the animals' reaction to innocuous touch (Figure 2A; Video 1; Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010) and illustrated in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: The nocifensive 'corkscrew' body roll is distinct from the animals' reaction to innocuous touch.
source: Importantly, this innate nocifensive behaviour, characterized by a 'corkscrew' body roll, can be quantified and is distinct from the animals' reaction to innocuous touch (Figure 2A; Video 1; Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010) that characterized the distinct behavioral responses.

claim: DEG/ENaC channels contribute to nociceptive mechanotransduction in invertebrates and mammals.
source: Degenerin/epithelial sodium channels (DEG/ENaCs) contribute to nociceptive mechanotransduction in invertebrates and mammals (Price et al., 2001; Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2010; Gorczyca et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014; Mauthner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Price et al., 2001; Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2010; Gorczyca et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014; Mauthner et al., 2014) documenting the role of DEG/ENaCs in mechanotransduction.

claim: Adhesion-type GPCRs (aGPCRs) participate in a vast range of physiological processes.
source: Adhesion-type GPCRs (aGPCRs) participate in a vast range of physiological processes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the diverse functions of aGPCRs.

claim: The frequent association of aGPCRs with mechanosensitive functions suggests that processing of mechanical stimuli may be a common feature of this receptor family.
source: Their frequent association with mechanosensitive functions suggests that processing of mechanical stimuli may be a common feature of this receptor family.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed association between aGPCRs and mechanosensitive functions.

claim: CIRL sensitizes sensory responses to gentle touch and sound by amplifying signal transduction in low-threshold mechanoreceptors.
source: Previously, we reported that the Drosophila aGPCR CIRL sensitizes sensory responses to gentle touch and sound by amplifying signal transduction in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Scholz et al., 2017) that demonstrated CIRL's role in low-threshold mechanoreceptors.

claim: CIRL adjusts nocifensive behaviour under physiological and pathological conditions.
source: Here, we show that Cirl is also expressed in high-threshold mechanical nociceptors where it adjusts nocifensive behaviour under physiological and pathological conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing CIRL's effects on nocifensive behavior under normal conditions and after paclitaxel treatment.

claim: Optogenetic in vivo experiments indicate that CIRL lowers cAMP levels in both mechanosensory submodalities.
source: Optogenetic in vivo experiments indicate that CIRL lowers cAMP levels in both mechanosensory submodalities.
evidence: The claim is inferred from optogenetic experiments using bPAC and the effects of adenylyl cyclase inhibitors.

claim: Contrasting its role in touch-sensitive neurons, CIRL dampens the response of nociceptors to mechanical stimulation.
source: However, contrasting its role in touch-sensitive neurons, CIRL dampens the response of nociceptors to mechanical stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that CIRL reduces nociceptor responses, in contrast to its sensitizing effect in ChO neurons.

claim: Rat nociceptors display decreased Cirl1 expression during allodynia.
source: Consistent with this finding, rat nociceptors display decreased Cirl1 expression during allodynia.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced Cirl1 expression in rat DRG neurons after CCI.

claim: cAMP-downregulation by CIRL exerts opposing effects on low-threshold mechanosensors and high-threshold nociceptors.
source: Thus, cAMP-downregulation by CIRL exerts opposing effects on low-threshold mechanosensors and high-threshold nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that CIRL lowers cAMP in both cell types but has opposite effects on their activity.

claim: The bipolar action of CIRL facilitates the separation of mechanosensory signals carrying different physiological information.
source: This intriguing bipolar action facilitates the separation of mechanosensory signals carrying different physiological information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CIRL's opposing effects on touch-sensitive neurons and nociceptors would enhance the contrast between these mechanosensory submodalities.

claim: Touch plays an important discriminative role and contributes to social interactions.
source: Touch plays an important discriminative role and contributes to social interactions (Abraira and Ginty, 2013; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Abraira and Ginty, 2013; McGlone et al., 2014) on the functions of touch.

claim: Nociception reports incipient or potential tissue damage and triggers protective behaviours.
source: Nociception reports incipient or potential tissue damage. It triggers protective behaviours and can give rise to pain sensations (Basbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Basbaum et al., 2009) on the function of nociception.

claim: Innocuous touch sensations rely on low-threshold mechanosensory neurons.
source: Whereas innocuous touch sensations rely on low-threshold mechanosensory neurons, noxious mechanical stimuli activate high-threshold mechanosensory neurons, i.e. nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the neural basis of touch sensation.

claim: Noxious mechanical stimuli activate high-threshold mechanosensory neurons (nociceptors).
source: Whereas innocuous touch sensations rely on low-threshold mechanosensory neurons, noxious mechanical stimuli activate high-threshold mechanosensory neurons, i.e. nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the neural basis of nociception.

claim: The activity of nociceptors can be increased through sensitization, e.g. upon inflammation.
source: The activity of nociceptors can be increased through sensitization, e.g. upon inflammation, and decreased through antinociceptive processes, leading to pain relief.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about nociceptor modulation.

claim: The activity of nociceptors can be decreased through antinociceptive processes, leading to pain relief.
source: The activity of nociceptors can be increased through sensitization, e.g. upon inflammation, and decreased through antinociceptive processes, leading to pain relief.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about antinociceptive mechanisms.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play an important modulatory role in nociceptor sensitization and antinociception.
source: In both cases, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play an important modulatory role.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about GPCR function in nociception.

claim: Receptors that couple to heterotrimeric Gq/11 or Gs proteins increase the excitability of nociceptors by activating phospholipase C and adenylyl cyclase pathways.
source: Receptors that couple to heterotrimeric Gq/11 or Gs proteins, like the prostaglandin EP2 receptor, increase the excitability of nociceptors by activating phospholipase C and adenylyl cyclase pathways, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about GPCR signaling in nociceptors.

claim: Gi/o-coupled receptors generally inhibit nociceptor signalling.
source: In contrast, Gi/o-coupled receptors, which are gated by soluble ligands like morphine and endogenous opioid neuropeptides generally inhibit nociceptor signalling.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Gi/o-coupled receptor function in nociceptors.

claim: In mammalian nociceptors, Gi/o-coupled receptors are located at presynaptic sites in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, at somata in dorsal root ganglia (DRG), and at peripheral processes.
source: In mammalian nociceptors, cell surface receptors that couple to Gi/o proteins are located at presynaptic sites in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where they reduce glutamate release, at somata in dorsal root ganglia (DRG), and at peripheral processes, where they suppress receptor potential generation (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018) on the localization and function of Gi/o-coupled receptors in nociceptors.

claim: Gi/o-coupled receptors at presynaptic sites in the dorsal horn reduce glutamate release.
source: In mammalian nociceptors, cell surface receptors that couple to Gi/o proteins are located at presynaptic sites in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where they reduce glutamate release, at somata in dorsal root ganglia (DRG), and at peripheral processes, where they suppress receptor potential generation (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018) on Gi/o-coupled receptor function.

claim: Gi/o-coupled receptors at peripheral processes suppress receptor potential generation.
source: In mammalian nociceptors, cell surface receptors that couple to Gi/o proteins are located at presynaptic sites in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where they reduce glutamate release, at somata in dorsal root ganglia (DRG), and at peripheral processes, where they suppress receptor potential generation (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018) on Gi/o-coupled receptor function.

claim: aGPCRs are associated with diverse human diseases, such as developmental disorders, defects of the nervous system, allergies and cancer.
source: Correspondingly, these receptors are associated with diverse human diseases, such as developmental disorders, defects of the nervous system, allergies and cancer (Hamann et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hamann et al., 2015; Scholz et al., 2016) on aGPCR-associated diseases.

claim: aGPCRs are not activated by soluble ligands, in contrast to most members of the GPCR phylum.
source: In contrast to most members of the GPCR phylum, aGPCRs are not activated by soluble ligands.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about aGPCR activation mechanisms.

claim: aGPCRs interact with partner molecules tethered to membranes or fixed to the extracellular matrix via their long, adhesive N-terminal domain.
source: Instead, aGPCRs interact with partner molecules tethered to membranes or fixed to the extracellular matrix via their long, adhesive N-terminal domain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about aGPCR structure and function.

claim: The arrangement of aGPCRs positions them as metabotropic mechanosensors, which translate a relative displacement of the receptor-bearing cell into an intracellular second messenger signal.
source: This arrangement positions aGPCRs as metabotropic mechanosensors, which translate a relative displacement of the receptor-bearing cell into an intracellular second messenger signal (Langenhan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Langenhan et al., 2016) proposing aGPCRs as metabotropic mechanosensors.

claim: The TRP channel subunits NOMPC, NAN, and IAV govern mechanosensation by larval ChO neurons.
source: The transient receptor potential (TRP) channel subunits NOMPC (no receptor potential, TRPN), NAN (nanchung, TRPV), and IAV (inactive, TRPV) govern mechanosensation by larval ChO neurons (Effertz et al., 2012; Lehnert et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Effertz et al., 2012; Lehnert et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013) on mechanotransduction in ChO neurons.

claim: The mechanically gated ion channel Piezo, the DEG/ENaC subunit Pickpocket, and the TRPN channel Painless are required for mechanical nociception in Drosophila.
source: The mechanically gated ion channel Piezo, the DEG/ENaC subunit Pickpocket, and the TRPN channel Painless, on the other hand, are required for mechanical nociception in Drosophila (Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012; Gorczyca et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014; Mauthner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012; Gorczyca et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014; Mauthner et al., 2014) on mechanotransduction in nociceptors.

claim: Enhanced nociceptor activity in mammals has been linked to elevated cAMP levels.
source: Matching our results in Drosophila, enhanced nociceptor activity in mammals has been linked to elevated cAMP levels.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cAMP's role in mammalian nociceptor sensitization.

claim: Mechanical hyperalgesia during inflammation involves cAMP-modulated HCN channels and sensitization of mammalian Piezo2 via PKA and PKC-based signalling.
source: For example, mechanical hyperalgesia during inflammation involves cAMP-modulated HCN channels and sensitization of mammalian Piezo2 via PKA and protein kinase C (PKC)-based signalling (Emery et al., 2011; Dubin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Emery et al., 2011; Dubin et al., 2012) on cAMP-dependent mechanisms of mechanical hyperalgesia.

claim: Gi/o-coupled receptors, such as opioid, somatostatin, and GABAB receptors, counteract cAMP-dependent nociceptor sensitization.
source: Conversely, Gi/o-coupled receptors, such as opioid, somatostatin, and GABAB receptors, counteract cAMP-dependent nociceptor sensitization (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Yudin and Rohacs, 2018) on Gi/o-coupled receptor function in nociceptors.

claim: Gβγ subunits of Gi/o-coupled GPCRs can directly interact with ion channels to suppress nociceptor signalling.
source: In addition to this second messenger pathway, Gβγ subunits of Gi/o-coupled GPCRs can directly interact with ion channels.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Gβγ subunit function.

claim: Nociceptor signalling can be suppressed via activation of G protein regulated inwardly rectifying K+ channels (GIRK) or by inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Thereby nociceptor signalling can be suppressed via activation of G protein regulated inwardly rectifying K+ channels (GIRK) or by inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Logothetis et al., 1987; Marker et al., 2005; Bourinet et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Logothetis et al., 1987; Marker et al., 2005; Bourinet et al., 2014) on ion channel modulation by Gi/o signaling.

claim: CIRL2 and CIRL3 promote synapse formation in the mouse hippocampus.
source: Recent work has identified that CIRL2 and CIRL3 promote synapse formation in the mouse hippocampus (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent work (Sando et al., 2019) on CIRL function in synapse formation.

claim: Stachel-dependent and -independent aGPCR activation triggers different downstream signalling pathways according to work in cell culture.
source: Work in cell culture has put forward a model in which Stachel-dependent and -independent aGPCR activation triggers different downstream signalling pathways (Kishore et al., 2016; Salzman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kishore et al., 2016; Salzman et al., 2017) on dual activation modes of aGPCRs.

claim: Many genes display altered expression in DRG neurons in neuropathy.
source: Many genes display altered expression in DRG neurons in neuropathy (Lopes et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Lopes et al., 2017) on gene expression changes in neuropathy.

claim: Receptors and ion channels involved in sensitization are upregulated in neuropathy.
source: For example, receptors and ion channels involved in sensitization are upregulated, whereas endogenous antinociceptive mechanisms, including opioid receptors and their peptides, are downregulated in certain neuropathy models (Herradon et al., 2008; Hervera et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Herradon et al., 2008; Hervera et al., 2011) on gene expression changes in neuropathy models.

claim: Endogenous antinociceptive mechanisms, including opioid receptors and their peptides, are downregulated in certain neuropathy models.
source: For example, receptors and ion channels involved in sensitization are upregulated, whereas endogenous antinociceptive mechanisms, including opioid receptors and their peptides, are downregulated in certain neuropathy models (Herradon et al., 2008; Hervera et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Herradon et al., 2008; Hervera et al., 2011) on gene expression changes in neuropathy models.

claim: Neuropathy not only enhances pro-nociceptive mechanisms but also decreases endogenous antinociceptive pathways.
source: Thus, neuropathy not only enhances pro-nociceptive mechanisms but also decreases endogenous antinociceptive pathways.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited literature on gene expression changes in neuropathy.

claim: IB4-positive non-peptidergic nociceptors have been linked to mechanical inflammatory hypersensitivity.
source: Our analysis of rodent DRGs indicates that neuropathy-induced allodynia correlates with reduced Cirl1 expression in IB4-positive non-peptidergic nociceptors (Fang et al., 2006), a class of neurons, which have been linked to mechanical inflammatory hypersensitivity (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fang et al., 2006; Pinto et al., 2019) on the function of IB4-positive neurons.

claim: Limited options for treating chronic pain have contributed to the current opioid epidemic.
source: Limited options for treating chronic pain have contributed to the current opioid epidemic (Skolnick and Volkow, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Skolnick and Volkow, 2016) on the opioid epidemic.

claim: Opioids are powerful analgesics but have severe side effects and lead to addiction mainly through activation of receptors in the central nervous system.
source: Opioids are powerful analgesics but have severe side effects and lead to addiction mainly through activation of receptors in the central nervous system.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about opioid pharmacology and side effects.

claim: The specificity theory defines nociceptors as a functionally distinct subtype of nerve endings specifically tuned to detect harmful, high-intensity stimuli.
source: The specificity theory, put forward more than 100 years ago (Sherrington, 1906), defines nociceptors as a functionally distinct subtype of nerve endings, which are specifically tuned to detect harmful, high-intensity stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to historical work (Sherrington, 1906) on the specificity theory of nociception.

claim: CIRL helps set the high activation threshold of mechanical nociceptors.
source: On the one hand, CIRL helps set the high activation threshold of mechanical nociceptors, while on the other hand, CIRL lowers the activation threshold of touch sensitive neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that CIRL reduces nociceptor excitability, and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: CIRL lowers the activation threshold of touch sensitive neurons.
source: On the one hand, CIRL helps set the high activation threshold of mechanical nociceptors, while on the other hand, CIRL lowers the activation threshold of touch sensitive neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work cited throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: CIRL's bidirectional adjustment moves both mechanosensory submodalities further apart and sharpens the contrast of mechanosensory signals carrying different information.
source: This bidirectional adjustment, attributable to cell-specific effects of cAMP, moves both submodalities further apart and sharpens the contrast of mechanosensory signals carrying different information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CIRL has opposite effects on the two mechanosensory submodalities.
